headline: California limits how employers use AI on workers

sources.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs laws to protect workers from AI risks (Associated Press, via ABC News)
California Bans Using AI to Monitor Workers' Brains, Emotions (Bloomberg Law)
California Lawmakers Try to Restrict 'Robo Bosses' (The Sacramento Bee, via Government Technology)
New California law limits how AI can be used to fire and discipline workers (video, ABC10)

chunks.text: California's governor signed several new laws on Wednesday, September 30, 2026. They {{rein in}} how California employers use AI on workers. Under one law, companies cannot {{turn firing decisions over}} to a computer alone. Another law bans AI tools that read workers' feelings. A third says employers must give [[written notice]] before they {{lay off}} large groups of workers because of AI. It was his last day to sign or reject bills this year.

verbs.wrong: To pay a worker more money
verbs.why: The new mayor promised to rein in city spending. Parents often try to rein in how much time kids spend online. California's new laws rein in how employers can use AI with their workers.

verbs.correct: To give control of something to another
verbs.why: She turned the store over to her son when she retired. The police turned the case over to a special team. Under one law, California companies cannot turn firing decisions over to a computer alone.

verbs.wrong: To print a new company rule
verbs.why: The factory laid off 200 workers last spring. The hotel had to lay off staff after a slow summer. Under a new California law, employers must give written notice before they lay off large groups of workers because of AI.

chunks.text: The law on feelings covers [[workplace surveillance]] tools. These include video and audio [[monitoring]], [[location tracking]] and time trackers. Employers cannot use these tools with AI to {{pick up on}} workers' emotions. Nor can they collect data on workers' [[brain activity]]. Companies can be [[fined]] up to $500 for each [[violation]]. The state's labor commissioner and public [[prosecutors]] can {{go after}} companies that break the rule. The governor asked lawmakers to {{clear up}} how far the law reaches.

verbs.correct: To notice something that is not obvious
verbs.wrong: To treat someone in an unkind way
verbs.why: Dogs can pick up on their owner's mood. The teacher picked up on the student's worry right away. Employers in California cannot use AI tools to pick up on workers' emotions.

verbs.correct: To try to catch or punish someone
verbs.why: The city is going after drivers who park in bus lanes. The bank went after customers who never paid their loans. Prosecutors in California can go after companies that use AI to read workers' feelings.

verbs.correct: To make something easier to understand
verbs.wrong: To make a rule last for more years
verbs.why: The manager sent an email to clear up the new schedule. Can you clear up what time the meeting starts? The governor asked lawmakers to clear up how far the new law on feelings reaches.

chunks.text: Under the firing law, a human must {{go over}} decisions made with [[automated systems]]. Labor unions supported the bill. The head of the state's union federation said decisions about a worker's [[paycheck]] or [[livelihood]] need human oversight. The state senator who wrote it said businesses should not depend entirely on machines to fire workers. The California Chamber of Commerce {{pushed back}} against the bill. Groups for restaurants, stores and [[grocers]] also opposed it. They warned that employers could {{end up}} facing [[costly lawsuits]].

verbs.wrong: To sign a paper for a worker
verbs.why: Please go over your answers before you finish the test. My lawyer went over the contract line by line. Under the new law, a human must go over firing decisions made with automated systems.

verbs.correct: To argue against an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To pay for a plan's costs
verbs.why: Parents pushed back when the school wanted longer days. Workers pushed back against the new dress code. The California Chamber of Commerce pushed back against the firing bill.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation
verbs.wrong: To win a case in court
verbs.why: If you don't save money, you could end up in debt. We got lost and ended up in the wrong town. Business groups warned that employers could end up facing costly lawsuits.

chunks.text: The governor {{turned down}} a broader bill on AI at work in 2025. He also [[criticized]] the Trump administration for not creating national AI rules. Instead, it reached a [[voluntary]] deal with the AI industry. He said states must {{step up}} without national leadership. His [[term]] ends in January, but he did not {{rule out}} [[special sessions]] of the legislature on AI.

verbs.wrong: To hide a bill from lawmakers
verbs.why: The bank turned down her request for a loan. The city turned down the plan for a new mall. In 2025, the governor turned down a broader bill on AI at work.

verbs.correct: To do more when it is needed
verbs.why: When the coach got sick, his assistant stepped up. Neighbors stepped up to help after the storm. The governor said states must step up because there is no national leadership on AI.

verbs.correct: To say something will not happen
verbs.wrong: To plan a trip to another state
verbs.why: The company has not ruled out more price increases. The coach ruled out any changes to the team. The governor did not rule out special sessions of the legislature on AI.

mainIdea.s: California now bars employers from letting AI alone fire workers or read their feelings on the job. Unions supported the new rules, while business groups warned of costly lawsuits.
mainIdea.why: The new laws ban AI tools that read emotions and require a human to check AI firing decisions. Unions backed the firing bill, and business groups pushed back.

mainIdea.s: Business groups backed new California limits on AI at work, including a ban on emotion tools. Labor unions opposed the laws and said human review of firings would cost workers jobs.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the sides are reversed. Labor unions supported the firing bill, and the California Chamber of Commerce and other business groups pushed back against it.

mainIdea.s: California has opened a state-run center to train workers whose jobs are at risk from AI. The program will offer free classes at community colleges across the state from next year.
mainIdea.why: There is no training center in this story. It is about new laws that limit how employers use AI on workers, including in firing decisions.

lines.text: Did you see California's new laws about AI at work?
A little. What do they actually do?
They {{rein in}} how bosses use it. A company can't {{turn firing decisions over}} to a computer anymore.
Good. A machine shouldn't [[have the final say]] on someone's job.
Right. Now a person has to {{go over}} the decision first.
Employers can't use AI tools to {{pick up on}} how workers feel. No reading emotions from cameras.
That sounds a lot like [[Big Brother]]. What happens if a company does it anyway?
Prosecutors can {{go after}} it, with fines of up to 500 dollars each time.
Not really. Business groups {{pushed back}}. They say companies could {{end up}} [[on the hook]] for costly lawsuits.
Is that [[over the top]], or a fair worry?
Hard to say. The governor {{turned down}} a broader version last year, so this one is narrower.
And there's a rule about layoffs too?
Yes. If a company plans to {{lay off}} lots of people because of AI, it has to warn them first.
Sounds like [[a step in the right direction]]. Will other states {{step up}} too?
A few have passed smaller rules so far. The governor says states have to act without national rules.
